note: AI-curated paraphrases of selected USDA Food Buying Guide passages, checked against the linked pages. This small collection contains general facts, not the complete guide or personal dietary advice. Program crediting rules apply only to the stated Child Nutrition Program context.

passages.title: USDA Food Buying Guide: Grains — definitions
passages.text: A whole grain contains the entire kernel: bran, germ and endosperm. Bran is the outer coating of a cereal grain such as wheat, rye or oats. Germ is the vitamin-rich embryo within the kernel. Flour is made by grinding grains. Enrichment means adding vitamins, minerals or protein to a food.

passages.title: USDA Food Buying Guide: Grains — examples
passages.section: Examples of foods creditable toward the grains component
passages.text: Examples of whole grains listed in the guide include whole wheat, brown rice, rolled oats and whole corn. Enriched grain examples include enriched flour, enriched rice, bread and pasta. The guide distinguishes whole grains from enriched grains in Child Nutrition Program meal planning.

passages.title: USDA Food Buying Guide: Vegetables — nutrients and variety
passages.text: Vegetables supply nutrients including potassium, dietary fiber, folate, vitamin A and vitamin C. The guide describes vegetable subgroups: dark green; red and orange; beans, peas and lentils; starchy; and other vegetables. Offering different vegetables provides a wider variety of nutrients.

passages.title: USDA Food Buying Guide: Vegetables — meal ideas
passages.text: The guide suggests adding vegetables to mixed dishes, such as tacos with black beans, corn or bell peppers. It also suggests green salads and including vegetables in meals and snacks. Fresh, frozen and canned vegetables are covered. These are general meal-planning examples; no individual blood sugar response is specified.

passages.title: USDA Food Buying Guide: Meats and Meat Alternates — examples
passages.text: The guide lists meat, poultry, fish, cheese, yogurt, soy yogurt, beans, peas, lentils, eggs, tofu, tempeh, nut and seed butters, nuts and seeds as meats or meat alternates. These are food examples used in Child Nutrition Program menu planning, not personalized protein targets.

passages.title: USDA Food Buying Guide: Meats and Meat Alternates — legumes
passages.text: Dry mature beans, peas and lentils can contribute as vegetables or meat alternates in Child Nutrition Programs. A single portion cannot count toward both daily meal components at once. Examples include kidney, pinto, white, black, lima and fava beans, soybeans, split peas and lentils. School weekly subgroup crediting has additional rules; this collection does not reproduce all those rules.
